text: His Jan. 8, 2026 "terms of engagement" for data centers say they "must pay for their own energy demand" (costs cannot be passed on to ratepayers), use closed-loop cooling and face penalties if promised local jobs do not appear. By September he was calling for federal standards and backing local and state moratoriums until then.
Released "AI Under Democracy", a 22-proposal AI platform built around democratic ownership and governance of AI, including support for public ownership of AI and protecting American jobs.
Reported to propose freezing the development of powerful AI systems and new data centers.

Endorsed the White House AI framework on Mar. 20, 2026, saying a consistent national framework would "supercharge innovation" and "shield communities from higher electric bills". In a Mar. 27 statement to Michigan Advance, said Michigan must be "competitive for new AI-supported jobs and investments ... while setting a responsible framework for safety and data privacy"; the paper described him as backing faster permits.

Called for a one-year moratorium on new data center construction in Michigan until "we establish a fair, transparent approval process that puts local communities first." Continued to oppose a federal ban.

Campaign platform calls for regulations that hold AI companies accountable while protecting workers, for AI companies to follow the same copyright laws as everyone else, and for limits on invasive workplace AI surveillance.
Proposed an "AI dividend": a tax on AI-attributable profits that would fund annual dividends to Americans and grants for entrepreneurs. The tax rate and eligibility rules are not specified.
Called for tighter regulation of data centers, describing his approach as a balance between welcoming the investment and protecting working people.

As Texas attorney general, opened an investigation into Meta AI Studio and Character.AI for possible deceptive trade practices and for misleadingly marketing themselves as mental health tools. In Sept. 2024 he reached a settlement with Pieces Technologies, a generative-AI health care company, over allegedly misleading claims.

Released a four-point AI data center plan calling for federal legislation to block Chinese technology in data centers and criminal liability for data centers that power AI chatbots that harm children, and backing Gov. Abbott's state-level plan.

As Michigan secretary of state, testified to the U.S. Senate Rules Committee that 2024 would be the first election cycle in which AI would be used to amplify election disinformation tactics "exponentially".
In a TV ad launched Sept. 13, 2026, called for a moratorium on data centers, an end to their tax breaks and stopping them from raising electric bills. Did not say how long a moratorium should last.

As a U.S. representative, voted on May 22, 2025 for the House budget bill (H.R. 1), which carried a 10-year moratorium on state and local enforcement of AI regulations; Michigan Advance argues it could have reached data center rules. The moratorium was removed before the bill became law.

His campaign said he supported a moratorium on new data centers until a local-control standard and protections for the environment and electricity bills were in place. On Face the Nation (Aug. 30) he said: "Our electricity bills can't go up. We must protect our water. We have to prevent pollution."

In the Oct. 6 debate said communities should decide on data centers ("My moratorium is local led, not Lansing led"); afterwards he told reporters "The moratorium should be imposed on Lansing, not the people" and ruled out a statewide moratorium.

At an Oct. 29 campaign stop in Bay County, said: "No new data centers until we have a plan to protect our communities," naming five concerns: local control, water, electricity bills, pollution, and building on brownfields rather than farmland.

Pledged an immediate moratorium on new data centers until the Legislature puts protections in place, an end to data center subsidies and a local say over projects. Goals include American union jobs, transparency (no NDAs for data center companies), data centers paying for themselves and protecting Texans' water and electricity costs. FOX 4 reported she called Gov. Abbott's pause "just words".

As governor-elect, told CNN the state will have laws to shield residents from data centers and that new projects should pause until then: "We will have laws to protect Texans, and we need to stop what we are doing with data centers until we have those protections."

Signed HB 149, the Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act (TRAIGA), effective Jan. 1, 2026. It bans a short list of AI uses, including AI-generated child sexual abuse material and government social scoring, and requires state agencies to disclose AI use to consumers.

Told state regulators and the grid operator ERCOT, in an Aug. 3, 2026 letter, to stop approving new data center grid connections until all data centers in the queue have been verified and audited for electricity and water use. Critics (Public Citizen) said the pause had no deadline and that projects generating their own power could bypass it.

Said he wants the Legislature to write his data center restrictions into law in 2027 and to give cities, counties and residents more authority over where data centers are built. His Sept. 21 release directing the state environmental agency (TCEQ) to halt data center permits said he would work with the Legislature to eliminate financial incentives for data centers.
Threatened to veto Connecticut's comprehensive AI bill (SB 2), which passed the state Senate 24-12 and then died in the House without a vote.
As a revised SB 2 advanced in 2025, his position was that AI regulation should fall to federal bodies such as Congress and the Federal Trade Commission rather than the state.
In his February State of the State address, said Connecticut would "slow down new data centers, unless they add more generation as well."

Signed SB 5 (Public Act 26-15), a broad AI law covering automated hiring decisions, consumer chatbots, frontier-model developers (including whistleblower protections), AI content provenance and platforms used by minors.

Said Connecticut is open to IT infrastructure but there is "no place" for massive data centers in the state, because they would raise residents' electric rates; proposals that bring their own water and electricity could be considered case by case, after review by the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority, with towns deciding.
As a state senator, was one of four senators to vote against SB 5, the 2026 AI law (passed 32-4), saying the issue is more properly handled at the federal level.
Called for ending tax breaks for large data centers and said they should "bring their own power if they are to plug into the grid," with guardrails on the industry. Does not want to ban data centers.

At a Brookings event, called restrictions on advanced chips Washington's main tool for prolonging America's frontier AI lead over China and said the U.S. should slow their spread to China for as long as it can.
At the same event, said of claims that China and others were stoking opposition to U.S. data centers: "I don't know if that's true, but it has a credible feeling to it."
On Face the Nation, raised concerns that Nvidia chips could reach China through intermediaries and questioned why the Commerce Department had not done more to stop the flow of the chips to China.
In a campaign email, argued the country faces an electricity problem driven by data centers, AI computing and electrification mandates.
Proposed expanding trade schools to provide "AI-proof" jobs, and requiring universities to disclose graduate salary ranges by degree.

Released an 11-point AI plan: fully fund and launch CalCompute (the public AI computing cluster called for in SB 53), independent audits of every AI system deployed by a state agency, stronger enforcement of California's AI safety laws, tracking AI's effects on jobs, and protecting children from risky AI products.

His campaign's AI plan says data centers should be powered with clean energy, cover the costs of their own energy needs and meet environmental disclosure requirements, in return for policy certainty for the industry.
His AI plan argues against "sweeping, preemptive regulation on evolving technologies" and would limit new AI rules to children's safety, fraud prevention and intellectual property.

Wants more electricity generation so that data center demand "would be less of an issue", and data centers sited farther from homes to limit noise. A policy analyst describes his plan as easing data center permits.
In the Sept. 30 debate, called for "an immediate pause on AI in the classroom", citing concerns about "cognitive stunting" in children's learning, and has called for a thoughtful evaluation.
Called AI "a major question of national sovereignty", as reported by AFP.

AI plan: build a sovereign European AI infrastructure that doubles "our" computing capacity in five years, raise the number of engineers trained each year from 40,000 to 100,000, create a right to retraining for threatened occupations, and back European champions such as Mistral through a "Buy European Tech Act" and joint purchasing by EU member states.

His campaign programme aims to make Europe a sovereign digital power, including in AI. At VivaTech in June 2026 he reportedly made AI sovereignty a central theme, which Ecostylia called an early credibility test of his campaign.
Wants France to control the entire AI value chain, treats AI training as a basic skill, and lists AI among his four "major projects" alongside schools, wages and borders.

His 56-page AI plan (July 2026) costs about €23 billion gross over five years, including about €11.6 billion of new AI investment (he had estimated about €25 billion in a July 7 interview). About €5 billion goes to AI in public administration: a single assistant for the public ("Marianne"), secure AI assistants for civil servants, 125,000 staff redeployed and 125,000 retirements left unfilled. It ties sovereign data center capacity to France's low-carbon nuclear fleet, favouring sites near existing plants.

Backs a moratorium on "non-sovereign" data centers built for foreign private companies subject to U.S. law. Asked whether he favours a moratorium and a slowdown of AI, he said yes, with safeguards written into a bill his movement is preparing.

His movement's parliamentary groups (June 1, 2026) proposed "a large public hub for digital technology and AI" and described data centers, computing and cloud as infrastructure as strategic as energy, transport and telecoms; his own 2027 programme proposes a public cloud of interconnected public data centers.

Her party's 2027 programme (Les Écologistes, July 2026) calls for assessing the impact of data centers and for planning their electricity use nationally and by territory, to anticipate conflicts with other uses, drinking water and land.
Her party's digital policy paper (Les Écologistes, July 2026) favors "smaller, specialized models open to inspection" rather than a handful of giant, opaque systems.

Filed a resolution in the National Assembly (registered Oct. 13, 2026) calling for a five-year moratorium on "non-sovereign" data center projects (foreign developers or end users), co-signed by individual Ecologist and Communist deputies. It also attacks the reduced electricity tax that data centers pay.

In a Fox Business appearance, Donalds said parents and the state of Florida should lead decisions on regulating AI, and that protecting children and making sure parents know what their children are doing with AI tools is the top priority.

A Florida Phoenix explainer on the stalled state AI Bill of Rights reported that Donalds thinks AI regulation should be left to the federal government, in line with President Trump's executive order on state AI laws. This is the outlet's description, not his own words, and it differs from his remarks in February and the fall.

During the general-election campaign, Donalds called for an AI bill of rights similar to the proposal Gov. Ron DeSantis introduced to protect children and families, and said there are common-sense guardrails around AI that Florida can lead on.

As a U.S. House member, Donalds introduced H.R. 9777, the Protecting Ratepayers Act, which would require hyperscale AI data centers to supply their own power generation and water instead of relying on public utilities, so their costs do not raise utility bills.

Donalds said he opposes a statewide moratorium on data centers but favors slowing construction of new ones, and that decisions on where data centers are built belong to local governments, with safeguards for water supplies, electric customers and neighborhoods.

Jolly said that if elected he would impose a one-year moratorium on data center construction to study environmental, health and economic effects, citing a lack of environmental and labor protections and privacy and safety concerns.
Jolly said a complete ban on data centers in Florida should be "on the table," and argued data centers depress nearby home values.

Jolly credited Gov. DeSantis for examining AI's effect on children, saying that until it is known AI cannot convince a young person to self-harm, "we need to pump the brakes." Reports say he has raised concerns about chatbots' effects on teenagers.
In a sit-down interview on AI and data centers, Jolly focused on protecting families and children and said AI should not replace teachers; he did not detail what regulations he would pursue.

As Florida attorney general, Moody joined a bipartisan coalition of 54 state and territorial attorneys general in a Sept. 5, 2023 letter asking Congress to create an expert commission on AI-enabled child exploitation and to expand child sexual abuse material laws to cover AI-generated material, including deepfakes.

The Senate voted 99-1 to strip a proposed 10-year moratorium on state AI laws from the budget reconciliation bill; Sen. Thom Tillis was the only senator voting no, which means Moody voted to remove the moratorium.

Moody has said consumers should not be left paying the costs associated with data centers, that environmental protections and local input are important, and that decisions about data centers belong to communities and states.

Nixon called for a moratorium on new data centers until more research is done and federal safeguards exist, telling Inside Climate News "There needs to be a moratorium" and "You cannot build any more data centers"; she also wants communities to receive economic benefits where data centers are built.
Nixon said she is not opposed to AI or technological innovation but wants tougher guardrails around privacy, employment and the construction of data centers.

At a Semafor event, Marshall said he supports the local data center moratoriums adopted by several dozen Kansas counties and that such decisions belong at the local level. He did not endorse a statewide moratorium like New York's but left open congressional action on national-security aspects of AI infrastructure.
Marshall said he opposes tax incentives for data centers, citing strain on local water and electricity supplies and the small number of permanent jobs they create.
Marshall said Kansans are "on fire" over data centers and called for keeping the U.S. ahead of China on AI while setting guardrails on the facilities.

Marshall and Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.) introduced the RESULTS Act, which would fund state education and workforce data systems so states can track and respond to job shifts from AI and other technologies.

Marshall voted for cloture on the House-passed Ratepayer Protection Act (H.R. 9340), which would have state utility regulators consider standards making data centers and other large users pay for grid upgrades. The motion failed 57-43. His vote is inferred from the tally (all Republicans voted yes) rather than seen by name.

Marshall voted for the Blackburn-Cantwell amendment that removed a 10-year moratorium on state AI laws from the budget reconciliation bill. The amendment passed 99-1, with Sen. Thom Tillis the only no vote.

Hamilton said local communities, not the state, should decide on data centers: "the heart of the data center debate is who decides, and that ought to be the local community." He said he does not favor a statewide policy on data center siting or permitting in Kansas.

Hamilton committed to making data centers pay for their own energy. In a voter-guide answer he said a data center's water use cannot come at the expense of drinking water or farm irrigation, or show up as higher bills for neighbors.
Collins cosponsored, with Sens. Marsha Blackburn, Maria Cantwell and Ed Markey, the amendment that removed a 10-year moratorium on state AI laws from the budget reconciliation bill. It passed 99-1.

Collins voted for the Ratepayer Protection Act, which would have state utility regulators consider standards making data centers pay for grid upgrades; the Senate motion failed 57-43. The American Prospect reports she also cosponsored the Senate bill.

In a debate Collins said Maine families and small businesses "are already paying some of the highest electricity costs in the nation" and cited the Ratepayer Protection Act. She has said data centers should be judged case by case, and at a forum she and Jackson agreed the facilities must not affect water use or raise electricity rates, with local agreements key.
Collins backs efforts to keep the U.S. ahead of China on AI and points to bipartisan work on AI scams and deceptive AI in elections; her campaign said it had not used AI in her re-election bid.

Collins joined Sens. Amy Klobuchar, Josh Hawley and Chris Coons in introducing the Protect Elections from Deceptive AI Act, which would bar materially deceptive AI-generated content depicting federal candidates in political ads.

In an "Agency over AI" plan released as a candidate for governor, Jackson proposed requiring AI companies that bring data centers to Maine to build their own power sources and pay for grid upgrades, and pledged to regulate data centers so they don't "raise power bills, drain the local water supply or make nearby homes unlivable." He said he would have signed the vetoed LD 307 moratorium.

The same plan would strip state contracts and tax breaks from major employers that attribute mass layoffs to AI, and called for safeguards against AI replacing Maine workers and for transparency when state government uses AI.

At the Oct. 13 debate Jackson said data centers built in Maine cannot raise electricity rates or hurt water quality, stressed union construction and maintenance jobs, and said "there has to be real parameters, real guidelines to how we're going to do this."
Jackson said the AI race needs to slow down or stop, and his campaign criticized Collins for backing Energy Secretary Chris Wright, a data center proponent.
Jackson criticized Gov. Janet Mills's April 2026 veto of LD 307, the state's temporary moratorium on large data centers, saying "She's concerned more about big business than she is about workers."

Husted introduced the Senate Ratepayer Protection Act, which would have state utility regulators consider standards so that data centers and other large electricity users pay for the energy and grid upgrades they require. Reps. Gabe Evans and Kathy Castor led the House companion.

After the House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act 417-3 on Sept. 16, Husted sought unanimous consent on Sept. 17 to pass it in the Senate and was blocked. A Sept. 30 cloture vote failed 57-43; Husted voted yes and blamed Senate Democrats.

Husted said data center siting should be a local decision and that "What we should do is protect the ratepayers from bearing the burden of the cost of building the electricity those data centers use."
Husted said Ohio's sales and use tax break for new data center construction, which he once backed, should no longer be awarded.

Husted introduced the Children Harmed by AI Technology (CHAT) Act (S. 2714), which would require AI companion chatbot operators to verify ages, block minors from sexually explicit content, notify parents about self-harm conversations and show recurring notices that users are talking to AI.

Husted and Sen. Andy Kim (D-N.J.) introduced a follow-up chatbot bill setting tiered federal standards for educational, companion and health chatbots used by minors, with age verification, parental controls and notification, crisis-referral rules, and enforcement by the FTC and state attorneys general.
Husted voted for the amendment that removed a 10-year moratorium on state AI laws from the budget reconciliation bill; it passed 99-1 with Sen. Thom Tillis the only no vote.
In an interview on his freshman priorities, Husted said he wants Congress to embrace AI and described innovation as a driver of economic growth and jobs.

Brown's campaign ads called Husted "the face of data centers in Ohio," saying he "cut sweetheart tax deals" and fast-tracked approvals "while ordinary residents watched their electricity bills explode."
Brown called for ending Ohio's data center tax breaks and said local communities should have a say on whether to allow data center construction.
In a campaign ad Brown promised to make data centers pay the full cost of their electricity use.

In an op-ed, Hinson argued that Washington's AI decisions will shape the world children grow up in, said AI risks should be scrutinized as carefully as its benefits are celebrated, and questioned whether current export controls go far enough to keep advanced AI chips away from China. She called for smart policy, strong enforcement and a ready workforce.

Sullivan joined Sen. John Cornyn and 11 other senators in introducing the FIGHT China Act, which would have Treasury prohibit or require notice of certain U.S. investments in Chinese technologies, including artificial intelligence and advanced semiconductors.
At a Senate Commerce Committee hearing titled 'Winning the AI Race,' Sullivan raised concerns that investment by American companies in Chinese AI could help make China's military more lethal.

The Senate voted 99-1 to adopt Sen. Marsha Blackburn's amendment removing a 10-year moratorium on state AI regulation from the reconciliation bill; Sen. Thom Tillis cast the only no vote, so Sullivan voted to remove the moratorium.

In his annual address to the Alaska Legislature, Sullivan listed Air Force data centers on Alaska bases, which would increase demand for natural gas, among recent progress, according to a Must Read Alaska summary. Newsweek separately reported that Sullivan petitioned to bring data centers onto Air Force and joint military installations and, with Gov. Mike Dunleavy, presented Alaska's cold climate and North Slope gas reserves as advantages for attracting AI data centers.

Sullivan's office said he authored provisions in the Senate Armed Services Committee's FY2027 defense authorization bill, including one directing the Department of War to set up a strategy and roadmap to reduce local community impacts while private data centers are built on military installations. The committee approved the bill 18-9.
Newsweek reported that Peltola has emphasized that local communities should have a voice in decisions on data centers and that data centers should pay their own way.

HB 149: Bans a short list of AI uses, including AI-generated child sexual abuse material and government social scoring, and requires Texas state agencies to disclose AI use to consumers. News reports describe it as a narrowed successor to an earlier proposal (HB 1709) that would have required impact assessments for high-risk AI.
S. 4214: Would prohibit building or upgrading AI data centers until laws regulating AI and AI data centers are enacted. Referred to the Senate Commerce Committee.
H.R. 9442: House companion to S. 4214, with about 20 cosponsors. Referred to the Energy and Commerce and Foreign Affairs committees.

S. 5658: Would prohibit building data centers on National Forest System land and land managed by the Interior Department, excluding specified Tribal lands. Referred to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee.

S. 5653 (passed as an amendment to H.R. 2347): Energy permitting package that bars utilities from recovering the extra retail costs of serving data centers and other large computing users from other customers. The White House says it puts the Ratepayer Protection Pledge into law; the Center for Biological Diversity calls it a giveaway to the data center industry.

H.R. 9340: Would have state utility regulators consider standards for making data centers pay for new generation and grid upgrades. Passed the House with bipartisan support; blocked in the Senate when cloture on the motion to proceed failed.
S. 5199: Would require large new electricity users such as AI data centers to pay the cost of the grid upgrades needed to connect them, rather than other ratepayers.

HB 5594-5596: Would pause data center approvals until April 1, 2027, including directing the Michigan Public Service Commission to halt approval of utility contracts or rates with data centers. Gov. Whitmer has said she will not sign a statewide moratorium.
SB 1018-1020: Senate package placing a moratorium on certain approvals for, and the operation of, new data centers.
HB 5396 (with HB 5397-5398): Would repeal the sales and use tax exemptions for data centers; companion bills address property tax treatment.

SB 296: Would pause new and expanded data centers for two years ("a utility may not energize a new or expanded electric service connection for a project"), then require approval by a local majority vote and a yearly payment, the greater of 2% of gross receipts or $10,000 per megawatt, shared equally among the host county's residents.
SB 293 (also HB 167): Would end existing data center sales tax breaks. SB 293 reportedly has 23 Senate authors; HB 167 is a House bill with the same aim.

SB 33, SB 35, SB 36: SB 33: data centers may not raise electricity costs for Texas residents. SB 35: ERCOT shares information on large-load customers, such as data centers, with the Texas Water Development Board. SB 36: limits data centers' eligibility for certain state and local incentive programs.

S. 146 (Public Law 119-12): Makes it a federal crime to knowingly publish, or threaten to publish, non-consensual intimate images, real or AI-generated, with conditions and exceptions set in the law. Covered platforms must remove such images within 48 hours of a valid request; they had a year to set up the process.
Number to verify: Would stop the December 2025 executive order targeting state AI laws from being carried out.
H.R. 3447: Would require advanced AI chips to carry security mechanisms that verify their location.
H.R. 6875: Would require the administration to notify Congress before approving advanced chip exports and let Congress block them.
H.R. 8170: Would require allied nations to match U.S. controls on exports of advanced chipmaking equipment to China.

SB 757-760: Would limit minors' access to AI chatbots and addictive social media feeds. SB 760 would bar chatbot products for minors unless they cannot encourage suicide, self-harm, harm to others, disordered eating or drug or alcohol use, and would let families sue, with a presumption that the chatbot caused the harm.
HB 4047-4048 (PA 11 and PA 12 of 2025): Add a civil cause of action and criminal penalties for non-consensual intimate deepfakes (HB 4047), with sentencing guidelines (HB 4048).
HB 5141, 5143, 5144: Require political ads generated wholly or substantially with AI to say so, and set penalties for distributing specified deceptive AI-generated election media.

SB 5 (Public Act 26-15): Broad AI law: using an automated employment decision tool is no defense to a discrimination claim; rules for consumer chatbots and AI companions; whistleblower protections and reporting channels at frontier-model developers; AI content provenance; protections for minors. Provisions phase in from Oct. 1, 2026 to 2028.
SB 2 (2025): Revised version of the 2024 comprehensive AI bill, including algorithmic-discrimination duties. Passed the Senate but was not taken up in the House after Gov. Lamont threatened a veto.
SB 2 (2024): Comprehensive AI standards bill. Passed the Senate 24-12 along party lines; the House Speaker did not call it for a vote after Gov. Lamont said he would veto it.

SB 245: Would have stopped new applications from July 1, 2026 to the 2021 program offering sales, use and property tax exemptions of up to 30 years for data center investments, while keeping existing agreements.
HB 5926: Would add a surcharge on electricity used by data centers to offset the public-benefits charge on household bills.
SB 1292: Would study energy efficiency for AI data centers.

To be filed: Senate Majority Leader Bob Duff proposes to pause new data centers until the state sets rules for power use, electricity costs and environmental protections, with a bill planned for the 2027 session. Some towns, such as East Lyme, have passed local bans.

S. 3852: Would bar private data centers drawing 20 megawatts or more (backup power included) from using grid power unless they rely on dedicated off-grid sources, starting 180 days after enactment. During a 10-year transition, existing centers can keep using grid power only while they hold a one-year federal "Zero Rate Effect Certificate". Planned sites would disclose estimated utility use for their first year and the next five; existing sites, current and next-five-year estimates plus up to five past years.
SB 1047: Would have required safety testing and added liability for developers of the largest AI models. Vetoed by Gov. Newsom.

SB 53: Transparency duties for the largest AI developers, a channel for reporting critical safety incidents to the Office of Emergency Services, whistleblower protections, and a framework for CalCompute, a public AI computing cluster. In force from Jan. 1, 2026.

SB 243: Requires safeguards for AI companion chatbots: disclosure that users are talking to AI, break reminders for minors and protocols for suicidal ideation. In force from Jan. 1, 2026. New York enacted similar safeguards earlier, in May 2025.
AB 1064: Would have restricted AI companion chatbots for children. Vetoed by Gov. Newsom.
SB 7: Would have limited employers' use of automated decision systems in employment decisions. Vetoed by Gov. Newsom; a version was enacted in 2026 as SB 947.

SB 947: Bars employers from relying solely on AI or automated decision systems to fire or discipline workers and requires human oversight of those decisions (the "No Robo Bosses Act of 2026", a narrower version of the vetoed SB 7).
AB 1331: Limits employers' use of AI-powered workplace surveillance, including restrictions on surveillance in workplace bathrooms.
AB 1883: Limits on collecting workers' data, including brain (neural) data, and on predicting workers' emotional states.
SB 1000: Updates rules on disclosing AI-generated content and its provenance.
SB 57: Began as a special electricity rate for data centers; narrowed to a Public Utilities Commission assessment of whether data center costs shift to other customers.

SB 886: Directs the Public Utilities Commission to set transmission-level tariffs for data centers by Jan. 1, 2028, so they pay to connect to the grid and for their power instead of general ratepayers. Part of a seven-bill data center package.
AB 2383: Data center tariffs must also cover wildfire mitigation and liability, electrification, environmental programs and other costs usually paid by distribution-level ratepayers.

SB 1168: Requires the Public Utilities Commission to assess options for rate structures that address the rate impacts of data centers (grid costs, buying power to serve added load, pressure on household rates). It does not itself set prices.

AB 1577: Requires data centers to report energy use and operating information to the Energy Commission and permitting agencies, with their effect on electricity demand covered in the state's Integrated Energy Policy Report.

SB 887: Prevents data centers from skipping the state-mandated environmental review for new projects. The package also requires developers to disclose projected water use and pay for water supply upgrades.

Regulation (EU) 2024/1689: Risk-based rules for AI across the EU: bans on certain uses, duties for high-risk systems and for general-purpose AI models, applied in phases. Member states such as France implement and enforce it rather than deciding whether to regulate.

Regulation (EU) 2026/1744: Delays high-risk AI Act duties (stand-alone systems to Dec. 2, 2027; AI in regulated products to Aug. 2, 2028), bans AI systems that generate non-consensual intimate images or child sexual abuse material (from Dec. 2, 2026), and simplifies rules for smaller firms. Systems generating synthetic content that were on the market before Aug. 2, 2026 get until Dec. 2, 2026 to meet the labelling duty; the timetable for general-purpose AI models is unchanged.

Proposition de loi (Senate): Lets large data centers be designated "projects of major national interest" by decree, which speeds up their approval, and strengthens local elected officials' role through territorial planning (SCoT). A lighter version was adopted after redundant articles were cut.

Law no. 2026-403 of May 26, 2026: Among many simplification measures, lets data centers that meet set conditions be designated projects of major national interest by decree, which speeds up siting and grid connection (Article 35), while allowing permits to be refused in water-stressed areas.

Government announcement: Before the February 2025 AI Action Summit, France was reported to be pledging a gigawatt of nuclear power for AI computing (TechRadar); the Élysée's summit document lists a France-UAE AI campus of up to one gigawatt. In March 2026 President Macron reportedly said France's nuclear plants let it open data centers and grow its computing capacity.

SB 6: Requires the Public Utility Commission to set interconnection standards and fees for large electricity users of 75 MW or more, such as data centers, and lets ERCOT curtail or disconnect them during grid emergencies.

SB 1964: Sets an AI code of ethics and minimum standards for state agencies and local governments that use AI in decisions affecting people's rights or benefits, and directs the Department of Information Resources to run a public-sector AI sandbox and write rules for higher-risk government AI.
SB 20: Creates criminal offenses for possessing, promoting or viewing obscene visual material, including AI-generated or computer-generated images, that appears to depict a child.

HB 581: Makes operators of websites and apps that use AI to create or alter sexual images liable when their tools are used to produce 'artificial sexual material harmful to minors' (computer-generated sexual material made with AI).
SB 441: Expands civil and criminal liability for creating or sharing nonconsensual sexually explicit images made with AI (deepfakes).

SB 338: Would set cooling and water-reporting requirements for large data centers on the ERCOT grid, with disconnection as a penalty, and would attach cooling, environmental cleanup and property-tax-abatement conditions to data center tax incentive agreements.
HB 4668: Would require large AI developers to adopt and publish safety protocols, run risk assessments and third-party audits, and protect whistleblowers, with civil penalties for violations.

HB 5899: Would have the Department of Technology, Management and Budget run a generative AI pilot program for state agencies, overseen by a three-member board, with limits on entering confidential data and human review of AI outputs.

HB 4536 (with HB 4537): Would bar health insurers from denying, modifying or delaying claims based on a review using artificial intelligence; companion HB 4537 applies similar limits to the state health department and its contracted health plans.

SB 761-763: Would deny water withdrawal permits to users consuming 2 million gallons a day or more (SB 761), require annual state reports on data center energy and water use (SB 762), and bar water utilities from passing data center infrastructure costs to residential customers (SB 763).

SB 1046-1051: Would require permits and hearings for users of more than 550,000 gallons of water a day, create a separate utility rate class so data centers pay their own power costs, set labor standards, limit officials' nondisclosure agreements with data centers, and require community benefit agreements before approval.

HB 6135-6142: Would create a large-load rate class for data centers (HB 6135), require closed-loop cooling or municipal water (HB 6138, 'Data Center Water Regulation Act'), require community benefit agreements (HB 6137), noise reports (HB 6139), limits on NDAs (HB 6140), labor standards (HB 6141) and decommissioning plans with financial assurance (HB 6142).

SB 1295 (Public Act 25-113): Amends the Connecticut Data Privacy Act to cover more businesses, let consumers opt out of automated decisions and profiling that have significant effects, require impact assessments for profiling (including minors' data) and add AI-related disclosure duties, effective July 1, 2026.

SB 4 (Public Act 26-64): Creates a data broker registry with a single state deletion portal, bans sales of precise geolocation data, restricts facial recognition and expands consumer rights over automated profiling and automated decision-making; most provisions take effect Oct. 1, 2026.

HB 5312 (Public Act 26-55): Lets a person harmed by the dissemination of an AI-generated (synthetically created) intimate image sue in Superior Court, requires covered platforms to remove such images within 48 hours of a valid request, and lets the attorney general seek civil penalties from noncompliant platforms; effective Oct. 1, 2026.

HB 5469: Would have required new customers of 50 MW or more, such as data centers, to get their power from a colocated or off-grid supplier and required utilities to file large-load tariff proposals with PURA by April 1, 2027; it cleared the Energy and Technology Committee on March 19, 2026 but died when the session ended.

SB 1119: Requires companion chatbot operators to assess child-safety risks every year, build in crisis protocols for suicidal ideation, offer parental controls and alerts if a child turns off safety settings, and submit to independent audits, with a private right of action for children harmed by violations.
AB 316: Bars a defendant that developed, modified or used an AI system from arguing in a civil suit that the AI acted autonomously to cause the plaintiff's harm; effective Jan. 1, 2026.

AB 621: Expands California's civil remedies for nonconsensual sexually explicit deepfakes, including claims for depicted minors and against those who knowingly facilitate or recklessly aid the conduct, such as services that keep deepfake pornography sites running.
SB 524: Requires law enforcement agencies to disclose on each page of an official report, including drafts, when the report was fully or partly written with AI; effective Jan. 1, 2026.

AB 93: Would have required data centers to estimate expected water use before applying for a business license and certify actual annual water use at renewal; Newsom vetoed it, saying he did not want to impose rigid reporting rules without knowing the impact on businesses and consumers.

S. 3062: Would bar AI companions for users under 18, require age verification and disclosure that chatbots are not human, and make it a crime to knowingly offer chatbots that engage minors in sexual content or encourage suicide; Senate Judiciary reported it 22-0 on Apr. 30, 2026 and it awaits a Senate floor vote.

S. 4591 / H.R. 8915: Would create a federal right to sue over unauthorized AI digital replicas of a person's voice or likeness; Senate Judiciary reported the Senate bill unanimously on June 18, 2026, but a unanimous-consent request to pass it was blocked by Sen. Cruz in October 2026.

H.R. 9925: Would set tiered federal transparency and safety rules for frontier AI developers, scaled to company size, including model cards, risk-management frameworks, independent audits and incident reporting, as a uniform national standard; it sits with House Energy and Commerce.

S. 4213: Would require data centers to report energy and water use to their states (and planned facilities to estimate five years of use), with states sending aggregated data to EPA, DOE and USDA for regional reports and the agencies able to fine noncompliant operators.

SB 484: Regulates large-scale data centers and other large-load electricity customers (50 MW or more), barring utilities from shifting the costs of serving them onto other customers, preserving local governments' authority to reject such facilities, and letting water regulators require alternative water sources. It also directs OPPAGA to study data center construction and operation and report by July 1, 2027.

SB 1118: Would have created a temporary public records exemption for information about a person's plans or interest in locating a data center in a county or municipality, tied to the effective date of SB 484 and subject to future legislative review and repeal.

HB 7031: Among other tax changes, limited the state sales tax exemption for data centers to facilities with at least 100 MW of critical IT load, with no grandfathering for smaller existing centers, and extended the deadline for exemption certificates from June 30, 2027 to June 30, 2037.

SB 482: Would have created a state 'Artificial Intelligence Bill of Rights,' including rules barring companion chatbots from interacting with minors without parental consent and requiring chatbots to disclose that they are not human. It was the legislative vehicle for Gov. DeSantis's AI proposal; House Speaker Daniel Perez said AI should be handled at the federal level.

Amended proclamation (executive action): Expanded the congressional redistricting special session to include protecting Floridians from AI harms, including an AI Bill of Rights, and public records exemptions for investigations of alleged AI harms.

SB 2-D: A refiled version of the regular-session AI Bill of Rights (SB 482) covering chatbot and consumer protections; a companion, SB 4-D, creating public records exemptions for AI-related investigations passed the Senate 33-4.

Governor's proposal (no bill number): Paired an AI consumer-protection package (deepfake and explicit-content protections, parental controls, limits on AI use of name, image and likeness, and a ban on "licensed" AI therapy) with a proposal to keep utility customers from paying for hyperscale AI data centers and let local governments reject them; the data center half became SB 484.

Governor's statement (no bill number): DeSantis said an executive order cannot preempt state AI laws and that only Congress can do so through legislation, and argued the order's language aligns with policies Florida is pursuing, such as child safety and data center rules.

HB 1161: Requires platforms that host user-generated content to set up a process, by Dec. 31, 2025, for people to request removal of nonconsensual altered sexual depictions (deepfakes) of themselves and to remove them within 48 hours of a valid request, with platforms facing lawsuits for noncompliance.

HB 527: Would have required a qualified human professional to make insurance claim denial or reduction decisions, barred AI output from being the sole basis for a denial, and required insurers to document AI use in claims-handling manuals.

HB 281: Would have barred licensed psychologists, clinical social workers, marriage and family therapists and mental health counselors from using AI to provide core therapy services, with some exceptions.

H.R. 9777: Would require large-scale AI data centers to obtain all their electricity and water from private sources rather than the public power grid or public water systems, turning a voluntary Trump administration initiative into a federal requirement.
